DMCA ANTI-CIRCUMVENTION AND REVERSE-ENGINEERING EXEMPTIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS DMCA ANTI-CIRCUMVENTION INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes 17 U.S.C. § 1201, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act's anti-circumvention provisions, which prohibit circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access to a copyrighted work and prohibit trafficking in tools designed to do so, along with the statutory exemptions most relevant to reverse engineering for interoperability (§ 1201(f)) and encryption research (§ 1201(g)). It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Acme, Inc.'s Acme Widget Manager, version 3.2. Section 1201 is a distinct part of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act from 17 U.S.C. § 512, the notice-and-takedown safe harbor addressed by this project's existing DMCA Takedown Notice and DMCA Counter-Notification documents: § 512 concerns a service provider's liability for hosting allegedly infringing material and the process for its removal or restoration, while § 1201 concerns circumventing technological access or copy controls, an entirely separate legal question that does not depend on whether any infringement notice has been sent. This Information Sheet is also distinct from, and does not restate, this project's existing trade secret documents: those describe when reverse engineering is or is not "improper means" under state trade secret law, a different body of law from the federal copyright statute described here. This document is a general informational reference describing what the statute says; it is not a court filing, a compliance certification, or legal advice about whether any specific technological measure, product, or activity involving Acme Widget Manager, version 3.2 complies with or falls within an exemption to § 1201.

THE GENERAL PROHIBITION ON CIRCUMVENTING AN ACCESS CONTROL
17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1)(A) states the statute's core prohibition: no person shall circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under Title 17 (copyright). This is an access-control prohibition — it applies to bypassing a measure that controls access to a work, and is analytically separate from § 1201(b), which instead addresses trafficking in technology designed to circumvent a measure that protects a copyright owner's specific exclusive rights (such as the right to copy) rather than access itself; § 1201(b) does not contain its own use-based prohibition parallel to (a)(1)(A). Section 1201(a)(2) separately prohibits manufacturing, importing, offering to the public, providing, or otherwise trafficking in technology, products, services, devices, or components that are primarily designed to circumvent an access control, that have only limited other commercially significant purpose, or that are marketed for circumvention use. A person injured by a violation of § 1201 may bring a civil action for that violation under 17 U.S.C. § 1203.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No person shall circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under this title."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, general prohibition on circumventing a technological access-control measure (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  "Any person injured by a violation of section 1201 or 1202 may bring a civil action in an appropriate United States district court for such violation."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1203(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, civil action for a violation of section 1201 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1203)
  Known gap: This describes only the general prohibition in (a)(1)(A) and the related trafficking prohibitions in (a)(2) and (b); it does not restate the statute's own periodic rulemaking exception described in (a)(1)(B) through (E) (under which the Librarian of Congress designates specific classes of works exempt from the (a)(1)(A) prohibition for renewable three-year periods), nor the further statutory exemptions in subsections (d) through (k) (for nonprofit libraries and archives, law enforcement, reverse engineering, encryption research, protection of minors, personally identifying information, and security testing), some of which are described in other clauses of this document. This clause also does not describe 17 U.S.C. § 1204's separate criminal penalties, which apply only to willful violations committed for purposes of commercial advantage or private financial gain and are not addressed by this civil-remedies-oriented document. Whether any specific measure "effectively controls access" to a specific work, or whether specific conduct "circumvents" it, are fact-specific applications of the statutory definitions addressed in a separate clause of this document.

THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITIONS OF "CIRCUMVENT" AND "EFFECTIVELY CONTROLS ACCESS"
Section 1201(a)(3) supplies the statutory definitions that determine the scope of the access-control prohibition in (a)(1)(A). "To circumvent a technological measure" is defined as descrambling a scrambled work, decrypting an encrypted work, or otherwise avoiding, bypassing, removing, deactivating, or impairing a technological measure, without the authority of the copyright owner. A technological measure "effectively controls access to a work" if, in the ordinary course of its operation, it requires the application of information, or a process or a treatment, with the authority of the copyright owner, to gain access to the work. Subsection (b)(2) defines the parallel terms used for the separate rights-protection trafficking prohibition in (b)(1) in similar, but not identical, terms — "to circumvent protection afforded by a technological measure" there means avoiding, bypassing, removing, deactivating, or otherwise impairing a technological measure, without the "without the authority of the copyright owner" clause that appears in the (a)(3)(A) definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "to “circumvent a technological measure” means to descramble a scrambled work, to decrypt an encrypted work, or otherwise to avoid, bypass, remove, deactivate, or impair a technological measure, without the authority of the copyright owner"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of "circumvent a technological measure" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  "a technological measure “effectively controls access to a work” if the measure, in the ordinary course of its operation, requires the application of information, or a process or a treatment, with the authority of the copyright owner, to gain access to the work."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of a measure that "effectively controls access to a work" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  Known gap: These are the statute's own codified definitions; this clause quotes them but does not summarize how courts have applied terms such as "effectively controls access" or "without the authority of the copyright owner" to particular technologies, because case-law research for this document was not completed (see the interoperability-exemption clause of this document for the specific reason). This clause also does not address whether a particular measure a reader may have in mind is, or is not, a "technological measure" that "effectively controls access" within the statutory definition — that is a technical, fact-specific question the statute's general definitions do not themselves resolve.

THE REVERSE-ENGINEERING / INTEROPERABILITY EXEMPTION IS CONDITIONAL, NOT AUTOMATIC
17 U.S.C. § 1201(f) creates a reverse-engineering exemption, but it is narrowly conditioned rather than a blanket permission to reverse engineer software. Under § 1201(f)(1), a person may circumvent an access-control measure protecting a computer program only where: (1) the person has lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of that program; (2) the circumvention is for the sole purpose of identifying and analyzing elements of the program necessary to achieve interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs; (3) those elements have not previously been readily available to the person engaging in the circumvention; and (4) the acts of identification and analysis, to the extent performed, do not themselves constitute copyright infringement. Section 1201(f)(2) separately permits developing and employing the technological means to circumvent — notwithstanding the trafficking prohibitions in (a)(2) and (b) — where necessary to enable that identification and analysis or to enable the resulting interoperability, again only to the extent doing so does not constitute infringement. Section 1201(f)(3) permits making the information or means acquired under (f)(1) or (f)(2) available to others, but only where done solely to enable interoperability of an independently created program, and only to the extent doing so does not infringe copyright or violate other applicable law. Section 1201(f)(4) defines "interoperability" to mean the ability of computer programs to exchange information, and of such programs mutually to use the information that has been exchanged.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "a person who has lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of a computer program may circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a particular portion of that program for the sole purpose of identifying and analyzing those elements of the program that are necessary to achieve interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, and that have not previously been readily available to the person engaging in the circumvention, to the extent any such acts of identification and analysis do not constitute infringement under this title."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(f)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, reverse engineering exemption — permitted act of circumvention (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  "the term “interoperability” means the ability of computer programs to exchange information, and of such programs mutually to use the information which has been exchanged."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(f)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of "interoperability" for the reverse-engineering exemption (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and summarizes the statutory conditions themselves; it does not resolve whether any specific act of reverse engineering satisfies them — questions such as whether a person's purpose was truly "sole," whether particular program elements were "previously readily available," whether a right to use a copy was "lawfully obtained," or whether resulting conduct "constitutes infringement" are fact-specific determinations that published case law addresses (courts have applied § 1201(f) and the related access-control prohibition in disputes involving, for example, video game console and emulator software and printer or garage-door-opener authentication chips). This document does not summarize that case law: CourtListener's case-law search tool was unavailable during this research session (its daily request quota, shared with earlier research in this project, had already been exhausted, returning a rate-limit error on the first attempted query), so no case-law citations were added rather than relying on unverified recollection of specific holdings. This is a statute-only treatment of § 1201(f) as a result.

THE ENCRYPTION RESEARCH EXEMPTION'S CONDITIONS
17 U.S.C. § 1201(g) creates a separate, similarly conditioned exemption for encryption research, defined in (g)(1)(A) as activities necessary to identify and analyze flaws and vulnerabilities of encryption technologies applied to copyrighted works, conducted to advance the state of knowledge in the field of encryption technology or to assist in developing encryption products. Under § 1201(g)(2), circumventing an access-control measure applied to a published work is not a violation of (a)(1)(A) in the course of good faith encryption research only if: the person lawfully obtained the encrypted copy, phonorecord, performance, or display; the act is necessary to conduct the research; the person made a good faith effort to obtain authorization before the circumvention; and the act does not constitute infringement or violate other applicable law, including the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act provisions in Title 18. Section 1201(g)(3) lists factors relevant to whether a person qualifies for this exemption, including how any resulting information was disseminated, whether the person is engaged in a legitimate course of study or is otherwise appropriately trained or experienced in encryption technology, and whether the person gave the copyright owner notice of the research findings. Section 1201(g)(4) separately permits developing and employing, or sharing with a collaborator, the technological means needed to perform or verify that good faith encryption research.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "it is not a violation of that subsection for a person to circumvent a technological measure as applied to a copy, phonorecord, performance, or display of a published work in the course of an act of good faith encryption research"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(g)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, permissible acts of encryption research (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  "the person made a good faith effort to obtain authorization before the circumvention"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(g)(2)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, encryption research condition — good faith effort to obtain authorization (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  Known gap: This describes only the encryption-research exemption; § 1201 contains several other, separately conditioned exemptions this document does not detail — including for law enforcement and government activity (§ 1201(e)), nonprofit library and archive access for acquisition decisions (§ 1201(d)), protection of personally identifying information (§ 1201(i)), and security testing (§ 1201(j)) — each with its own specific conditions. Whether a particular research activity was conducted in "good faith," was "necessary," or involved a sufficient "good faith effort to obtain authorization" are fact-specific determinations this clause does not resolve for any particular activity.

TWO DIFFERENT BODIES OF LAW: DMCA CIRCUMVENTION VERSUS TRADE SECRET REVERSE ENGINEERING
17 U.S.C. § 1201 and California trade secret law address reverse engineering from different legal angles and can reach different results for the same underlying conduct. California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act, Civil Code § 3426.1(a), defines "improper means" for purposes of trade secret misappropriation to include theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, and espionage, but expressly states that reverse engineering or independent derivation alone is not considered improper means — meaning reverse engineering a product to learn how it works is not, by itself, trade secret misappropriation under California law. Section 1201, by contrast, is a federal copyright statute concerned with a different act: circumventing a technological measure that controls access to a copyrighted work. It does not ask whether the underlying information is a trade secret, and it is not excused merely because the reverse engineering is directed at learning non-secret or independently discoverable information. As a result, an act of reverse engineering that trade secret law would not treat as improper may still involve circumventing a technological access control within the meaning of § 1201(a)(1)(A) — and would require satisfying § 1201(f)'s own, separate conditions (described in another clause of this document) to fall within that statute's reverse-engineering exemption, rather than relying on the trade secret law's more permissive treatment of reverse engineering.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Improper means” includes theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, or espionage through electronic or other means. Reverse engineering or independent derivation alone shall not be considered improper means."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, definition of "improper means" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.1.)
  "No person shall circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under this title."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, general prohibition on circumventing a technological access-control measure (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/1201)
  Known gap: This clause states an analytical distinction between two separately sourced bodies of law — federal copyright law under § 1201 and California's state trade secret statute — based on each statute's own text; it does not resolve whether any specific act of reverse engineering would, in fact, violate § 1201, satisfy the § 1201(f) exemption, or constitute or avoid trade secret misappropriation, which depends on the specific technology, conduct, and agreements involved. This project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document addresses the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's parallel "improper means" definition (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)), which is worded similarly to California's statute but is a distinct federal statute not quoted again here to avoid duplication.
